title: The first-born before the waters
theme: The one who sees the first-born — born of tapas, born before the waters — dwelling in the cave with the elements, sees this. This is that.

words.role: relative pronoun (the one born before the waters)
verb of the first relative clause
verb of the second relative clause

sandhi.type: aḥ → o; m before a vowel
sandhi.rule: The ru of -aḥ becomes u before a voiced consonant, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), and a + u → o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः); final m stays before a vowel.
Final m stays m before a vowel; before a consonant it becomes anusvāra, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).
yaḥ → yo before a voiced consonant, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च); the s of bhūtebhiḥ becomes ru, P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः), heard as r before a voiced sound.

morphology.note: Vedic instrumental plural in -ebhiḥ for classical bhūtaiḥ (so Śaṅkara glosses it).
Imperfect middle of jan ‘be born’. Madhva takes it in a causative sense, ‘caused to be born’, as with an unexpressed causative suffix, «अन्तर्णीतणिच्»: the Lord who produced the first-born.
Imperfect middle of paś (dṛś) with vi; Śaṅkara takes the past as present, ‘who sees’.
Ablative plural of ap ‘water’ (stem ad- before bh), the standard of comparison with pūrvam, ‘before the waters’.

translation.literal: ‘[He] who [sees] the one born first from tapas, who was born before the waters, dwelling, having entered the cave, with the elements — who saw [him sees this]. This, truly, is that.’
translation.readable: ‘Whoever sees the first-born — born of tapas before the waters came to be, who has entered the cave of the heart and dwells there with the elements — sees this. This is that.’

anvaya: यः तपसः पूर्वम् जातम्, [यः] अद्भ्यः पूर्वम् अजायत, [तम्] गुहाम् प्रविश्य भूतेभिः [सह] तिष्ठन्तम् यः व्यपश्यत, [सः एतत् एव पश्यति] । एतत् वै तत् ॥
syntax: Two relative clauses, each opening with yaḥ, and a refrain; the construction is loose and the commentators distribute the relatives differently (see ambiguities). jātam and tiṣṭhantam are the accusatives of what is seen; bhūtebhiḥ marks accompaniment.

ambiguities.topic: Who is born, and who sees?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the seeker, «यः कश्चिन्मुमुक्षुः», who sees the first-born Hiraṇyagarbha, «उत्पन्नं हिरण्यगर्भम्», born of Brahman before the five elements, dwelling in the heart; whoever sees so sees the Brahman under discussion, «स एतदेव पश्यति — यत्तत्प्रकृतं ब्रह्म». Raṅgarāmānuja: the four-faced Brahmā is the first-born, and the one who ‘saw’ him is the Supreme, who looked on him meaning him to be creator of the world, «अयं सकलजगत्स्रष्टा स्यात् इति कटाक्षेण ऐक्षत इत्यर्थः». Madhva: Viṣṇu produced Brahmā before the waters and before the Śiva called tapas, in a verse he cites, «पूर्वं यो जनयामास पूर्वजातं चतुर्मुखम्».

Śaṅkara: Brahman, whose tapas is knowledge, «ज्ञानादिलक्षणाद्ब्रह्मण इत्येतत्». Raṅgarāmānuja: by mere resolve, «संकल्पमात्रादेव». In Madhva’s cited verse tapas is a name of Śiva, «तपोनाम्नः शिवादपि».

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Two half-lines of 16 syllables, four pādas of eight, then the refrain etad vai tat, four syllables.

beginner: This verse is one of the hardest in the Kaṭha, and the old commentators read its grammar differently. All agree it speaks of the 'first-born': the first being to appear at the start of creation, before even the waters, born from the creative power the Upaniṣads call tapas — literally 'heat', the concentrated effort of creation. This first-born is said to have entered the 'cave', the inner space of the heart, and to dwell there along with the elements that make up a living body. For Śaṅkara the point is that whoever sees this cosmic first-being dwelling in the heart sees the very Brahman the teaching is about. For Raṅgarāmānuja and Madhva the first-born is the creator god Brahmā, and the one who 'saw' or brought him forth is the Supreme Lord. The refrain closes it again: this is that.
analogy: A family tree traced back to its first ancestor, only to find that same ancestor alive in each descendant.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Whoever sees the first-born, born of tapas before the waters, dwelling in the cave with the elements, sees this; this is that.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: the verse shows that the one described as the inward self and the Lord is the self of all, «स सर्वात्मेत्येतद्दर्शयति». The first-born is Hiraṇyagarbha, who after producing the bodies of gods and others entered the cave of all beings, the space of the heart, «देवादिशरीराण्युत्पाद्य सर्वप्राणिगुहां हृदयाकाशं प्रविश्य».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: He reads the first-born as Brahmā, born from the waters in the account of the Manusmṛti he quotes, «तस्मिन् जज्ञे स्वयं ब्रह्मा सर्वलोकपितामहः», and the one who saw him as the Supreme, who looked on him to make him creator.

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Madhva cites a verse (with «इति च», no source named) in which Viṣṇu, before the waters, produced the four-faced first-born and sees himself in the heart with all beings, «यः पश्यति सदा विष्णुस्स एष हृदि संस्थितः». Unlike Indra and the other gods, born again from Kaśyapa, Brahmā is not born of the Lord in that way, «न तथा भगवतो ब्रह्मा»; ajāyata means ‘caused to be born’.

advaita.text: Whoever sees Hiraṇyagarbha, the first-born, dwelling in the heart sees the very Brahman under discussion, «यत्तत्प्रकृतं ब्रह्म»: the self of all.

visistadvaita.text: The first-born is Brahmā; the Supreme saw him in the heart, endowed with body and senses, and made him creator, «अयं सकलजगत्स्रष्टा स्यात् इति कटाक्षेण ऐक्षत इत्यर्थः».

dvaita.text: Viṣṇu produced the four-faced first-born before the waters, «पूर्वं यो जनयामास पूर्वजातं चतुर्मुखम्» (a verse he cites), and dwells in the heart; ajāyata is causative.

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara makes the seer a seeker and the seen the cosmic first-born, finally Brahman; Raṅgarāmānuja and Madhva make the first-born Brahmā and the subject the Lord who looked on him or produced him. The verse’s two relatives allow both.

parallels.quote: यो वेद निहितं गुहायां परमे व्योमन्
parallels.note: The Taittirīya’s Brahman ‘placed in the cave, in the highest heaven’.

contemporary.text: The verse ties the beginning of everything to what dwells in each heart now; the question of origins becomes a question about what is present. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: What is the oldest thing you can think of that is still present in you?
reflect.deeper: Why might the Upaniṣad place the first-born of creation in the cave of the heart?
reflect.practice: Read the verse slowly twice, once as Śaṅkara reads it and once as Raṅgarāmānuja does, and notice how the picture changes.

flags.note: The two relative clauses are distributed differently by each commentator; the translation follows Śaṅkara’s, with the others under ambiguities.
